Solution:
Consider a river crossing problem defined by the inputs n, k, and an n-vertex
graph G. There are n passengers to be transported across a river by a pilot, Charon. The
ferry has a maximum capacity of k individuals, which must include Charon to operate the
vessel. The graph G defines conflict constraints: an edge between two vertices indicates
that the corresponding passengers are enemies. The safety conditions dictate that no pair
of enemies may be present together on either riverbank unless Charon is also present at
that location. Prove that the decision problem of determining whether a valid sequence of
crossings exists to transport all n passengers across the river is NP-hard.
Theorem 1. The decision problem of determining whether a valid sequence of crossings
exists for the river crossing problem with parameters (n, k, G) is NP-hard.
Proof. We prove NP-hardness by reduction from the 3-Coloring problem, which is known
to be NP-complete.
First, let us formalize the river crossing problem:
• State: A configuration (L, R, c) where L ⊆V (G) are passengers on the left bank,
R ⊆V (G) are passengers on the right bank, and c ∈{left, right} indicates Charon’s
position, with L ∩R = ∅and L ∪R = V (G).
• Initial State: (V (G), ∅, left)
• Goal State: (∅, V (G), right)
• Valid State: A state (L, R, c) is valid if:
– When c = left: R forms an independent set in G (no edge between any two
vertices in R)
– When c = right: L forms an independent set in G
• Transition: From state (L, R, left), Charon can move to (L \ S, R ∪S, right) for any
S ⊆L with |S| ≤k −1. Similarly from (L, R, right) to (L ∪S, R \ S, left) for S ⊆R
with |S| ≤k −1.
Given: An undirected graph H = (VH, EH) with |VH| = m.
Question: Is H 3-colorable?
Construction: We construct an instance of the river crossing problem as follows:
• Set n = 3m (we create three copies of each vertex in H)
• For each vertex v ∈VH, create three passengers: v(1), v(2), v(3)
• Define the conflict graph G = (VG, EG) where:
VG = {v(i) : v ∈VH, i ∈{1, 2, 3}}
EG = {(u(i), v(j)) : (u, v) ∈EH, i = j} ∪{(v(i), v(j)) : v ∈VH, i ̸= j}
• Set k = m + 1 (Charon plus m passengers)
1

Intuition:
• Each vertex v ∈VH has three copies corresponding to three potential colors
• Edges (v(i), v(j)) for i ̸= j ensure that only one copy of each vertex can be selected
• Edges (u(i), v(i)) when (u, v) ∈EH ensure that adjacent vertices in H don’t receive the
same color
Claim 1. H is 3-colorable if and only if there exists a valid crossing sequence for the con-
structed instance.
(⇒) If H is 3-colorable:
Suppose χ : VH →{1, 2, 3} is a proper 3-coloring of H. For each color i ∈{1, 2, 3},
define:
Ci = {v(i) : v ∈VH, χ(v) = i}
Note that |C1| + |C2| + |C3| = m since each vertex gets exactly one color, and |Ci| ≤m
for each i. Also, each Ci is an independent set in G because:
• For u, v ∈VH with χ(u) = χ(v) = i, if (u, v) ∈EH, then (u(i), v(i)) ∈EG, contradicting
that χ is proper
• No Ci contains two copies of the same vertex
Consider the following crossing sequence:
1. Charon takes all passengers in C1 from left to right. This is valid since |C1| ≤m < k,
and the remaining passengers C2 ∪C3 on the left form an independent set (no edges
between them in G since they’re from different color classes and correspond to different
vertices of H).
2. Charon returns alone to the left. The right bank now contains C1, which is independent.
3. Charon takes all passengers in C2 from left to right. The remaining C3 on the left is
independent.
4. Charon returns alone. The right bank contains C1 ∪C2, which is independent.
5. Charon takes all passengers in C3 to the right, completing the transport.
At each step, the validity condition is satisfied.
(⇐) If a valid crossing sequence exists:
Suppose there exists a valid sequence transporting all passengers. Consider the state
after the first trip where Charon reaches the right bank with some set S ⊆VG. At this
point:
• S contains at most k −1 = m passengers
• VG \ S must be an independent set in G
2

By the structure of G, for VG \ S to be independent:
• For each v ∈VH, at least one copy v(i) must be in S (otherwise v(i), v(j) ∈VG \ S for
i ̸= j, creating an edge)
• Since |S| ≤m and there are m vertices in VH, exactly one copy of each vertex is in S
Thus, S = {v(χ(v)) : v ∈VH} for some function χ : VH →{1, 2, 3}. Since VG \ S is
independent, for any edge (u, v) ∈EH and any i ∈{1, 2, 3}, we cannot have both u(i), v(i) ∈
VG \ S, which means χ(u) = i or χ(v) = i. Therefore, χ(u) ̸= χ(v), making χ a proper
3-coloring.
Since 3-Coloring is NP-complete and we have shown a polynomial-time reduction to the
river crossing problem, the river crossing problem is NP-hard.
3
fields.explanation: The edgeless source H on2 vertices, six copied passengers, two disjoint conflict triangles and total boat capacity3 are unchanged. The repair uses at most2 passengers because the third seat is Charon. It proves the first unattended bank cannot be independent; the old permissive3-passenger model and incorrectly defined Ci are removed. The selected theorem certifies the source-qualified primary counterexample. Historical auxiliary sweeps are not silently promoted to universal statements. The original family argument also survives with the source capacity convention: for every m≥2, choose the edgeless H on m vertices. The conflict graph consists of m disjoint triangles, so every independent set has at most m passengers and any first trip must remove at least 3m−m=2m passengers. Capacity m+1 including Charon permits only m passengers, which is insufficient. These are distinct counterexamples of unbounded size.
fields.flaw: Keep H as the edgeless graph on two vertices a,b. Its proper 3-coloring produces six passengers a(1),a(2),a(3),b(1),b(2),b(3), with conflict graph the disjoint union of their two triangles. The source boat capacity is k=m+1=3 individuals including Charon, hence at most two passengers. Any first trip therefore leaves at least four passengers unattended. An independent set in these two triangles has at most two vertices, so every possible first trip violates the unattended-bank condition. The source Claim 1 says the constructed instance is feasible for this 3-colorable H; it is not. The original family argument also survives with the source capacity convention: for every m≥2, choose the edgeless H on m vertices. The conflict graph consists of m disjoint triangles, so every independent set has at most m passengers and any first trip must remove at least 3m−m=2m passengers. Capacity m+1 including Charon permits only m passengers, which is insufficient. These are distinct counterexamples of unbounded size.
